summary:
Jewish Autonomous Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) contains no oblast-specific information beyond that national framework, and the division is assessed at the national score. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. No lawful route exists for a visitor or resident to align an official gender marker with their presentation.

The expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything explicitly "justifying" gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and repeated offences risk criminal prosecution. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in November 2023. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison; participation carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising 6-10 years. Charges are brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The UK Home Office affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement in Russia, a figure that covers residents as well as those encountered by police in public and online.

Human Rights Watch documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media. The same accounting records 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22, indicating that residents face materially higher exposure to fines than they did three years earlier.

Residents lose access to legal gender recognition and to trans-specific healthcare under the 2023 legislation, and cannot marry a same-sex partner. The UK Home Office note records no division-specific information for Jewish Autonomous Oblast beyond this national position, so residents of the oblast are assessed against the same standards as the rest of the country.

LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, are recognised by the UK Home Office as constituting a particular social group under the refugee convention, which governs how UK asylum claims from Russian nationals are assessed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory reports enforcement activity, raids, detention conditions or document checks specific to Jewish Autonomous Oblast. The assessment rests on the national framework, and oblast-level enforcement patterns remain unresolved.

Whether border or entry screening at points of access to the oblast questions travellers about gender markers, prior legal gender change or medical history is not sourced.

The penalty ranges of 2-6 years' imprisonment for participating in the designated extremist movement and 6-10 years for organising it are stated in the record for this division but are not independently confirmed in the two source notes cited here; the upper figure of 12 years reported by Human Rights Watch reflects sentences actually imposed.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian took place near Novosibirsk, not in Jewish Autonomous Oblast, and is cited only as evidence of the national pattern of physical coercion against transgender people.

The currency conversion of 400,000 rubles to about £3,600 and the US State Department advisory level are dated to their cited sources and may have moved since; both remain unresolved against current figures.
